text: This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya.

On today's Roundtable, campaign ads get nasty. Rush Limbaugh apologizes after saying Michael J. Fox played up his Parkinson's tremors in a Missouri ad. And in Tennessee, TV spots dog Senate hopeful Harold Ford, Jr. for his playboy image.

Joining us today from our NPR headquarters in Washington, D.C., we've got Yvonne Bynoe, author of the book Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture, along with Ron Christie - he's the vice president counsel for the lobbying firm D.C. Navigators and former special assistant to President Bush. In our New York bureau, we've got Walter Fields, CEO and publisher of the NorthStarNetwork.com.

Welcome to all of you, and let's start with the negative ads. Actor Michael J. Fox has lobbied for stem cell research for years. He struggled with Parkinson's for years. And this campaign season, he's appeared in several ads for candidates backing stem cell research, which is controversial. This one ran in Missouri.

Mr. MICHAEL J. FOX (Actor): As you might know, I care deeply about stem cell research. In Missouri, you can elect Claire McCaskill, who shares my hope for cures. Unfortunately, Senator Jim Talent opposes expanding stem cell research. Senator Talent even wanted to criminalize the science that gives us a chance for hope. They say all politics is local, but it's not always the case. What you're doing in Missouri matters to millions of Americans. Americans like me.

And when you hear that ad - of course we can't show it on the radio -you hear what sounds like cloth rubbing. He is twitching and bobbing and weaving. And then talk show host Rush Limbaugh had this to say about the ad after it aired.

speaker_label: Mr. RUSH LIMBAUGH (TV Show Host, The Rush Limbaugh Show)
text: This is really shameless, folks. This is really shameless of Michael J. Fox. Either he didn't take his medication or his acting, one of the two.
All right. I'm going to go to you, Ron Christie. What are we to make of this?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Unfortunately, I think that Michael J. Fox has really been a hero to so many Americans in what has happened to him, and we've seen the degenerative nature of his disease. I think it's painful for all of us to watch.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: But Mr. Fox put himself in the political discourse when he shot spots in Missouri and in Maryland and a couple of other states around the country talking about stem cell research. I think if you listen to what Mr. Fox actually said, as it relates to Mr. Talent's record, I think his comments are a little bit misleading. He suggests, Mr. Fox does, that Mr. Talent is against stem cell research, and that is just not true.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Senator Talent is against a particular form of embryonic stem cell research, which would destroy embryos. And Mr. Fox does not mention that in that 30-second television spot.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: But looking at what Mr. Limbaugh had to say, I think, again, it's unfortunate. Mr. Limbaugh said that either Mr. Fox had not taken his medication or was exaggerating or acting for the benefit of the cameras. Mr. Limbaugh apologized. I think that is not a proper course of action for one who is such a powerful commentator to be saying on television when there are so many millions of Americans who suffer from the disease.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: But fair or unfair, Mr. Fox put himself in a political crosshairs when he cut those spots for television.

Yvonne, embryonic stem cell research is often compared to abortion in the sense that you have embryos usually left over from unused fertility treatments that go into this research. And that's part of the debate over this. I don't want to get too deep into stem cell research, but what do you think of the ad and the controversy?

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: Well, I guess from where I stand, this has less to do with Michael J. Fox and his inserting himself into political dialogue than it does for Rush Limbaugh to now appear that he has some medical expertise, which he does not.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: He did not really address the fact of what Mr. Fox said in terms of his support of one candidate over the other one. I think, given his own track record and given his own personal foibles that he should have been more considerate of what he was saying.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: And I think that's a - we're having a different debate here. This is not about a debate of ideas, whether one guy's idea is better than the other one. These are personal attacks. And I think that the public is just simply getting tired of whether it's political pundants or whether its political candidates skirting the issue at hand - the substantive issue - just to lob grenades at a particular person.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: So certainly, Michael J. Fox inserts himself in a particular political dialogue, and I think Rush Limbaugh certainly could have debated whether or not his position was correct in terms of these particular political stances.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: But to start talking about whether or not the man was off his medication and whether or not he was acting for the camera, I think that's an abominable thing. And he's playing to a particular audience that perhaps appreciates that type of dialogue.

Walter, you know, in some ways Rush Limbaugh seems like a Teflon guy because he had, you know, well-publicized problems with possession of OxyContin, which is a powerful medical narcotic that apparently he wasn't supposed to have. And now he's talking about Michael J. Fox's medication. I mean, does it really matter that he himself, Rush Limbaugh, has a questionable record? Or is he just Teflon and able to roll like that?

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: Well, it's the era of new media. What Rush Limbaugh has is an audience, and it makes money for the owners of his syndication. You know, I think it's one thing if he talked about accuracy of the ad, which he didn't do. I mean, this was a personal attack, and its just part of sort of the rhetoric we hear in talking head media. You know, it's rarely steeped in truth, though it's presented as such.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: So I think, you know, Rush Limbaugh - he is not Teflon. Clearly, he was criticized for his own personal failures. But what we have here is a situation where we have a niche audience. And Rush Limbaugh makes money, and I think he'll always be on the air as long as he makes money. The day that he stops making money, we won't hear from this man again. I mean, that's the sad truth of it all.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: So I think we, you know, we're splitting hairs here. Let's not talk about the accuracy of Michael J. Fox's statements, unless Rush Limbaugh directly addressed that. He didn't do that. This was a personal attack that suggested that this person was faking an illness, which I find incredible that anyone could even find a way to defend that attack.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: And I think it's tragic, because I think millions of Americans - Republican and Democrats - probably find this to be a very shameful expression from Mr. Limbaugh.

And along those lines, I went on YouTube, which has both of the videos - the video of Rush Limbaugh and the video of Michael J. Fox. And a lot of people were, you know, saying across partisan lines that they didn't like the attack.

But let's move on to another attack ad, because it's that season. Just like you have the holidays, you have attack ad season, and we're deep in it. So you've got Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Harold Ford, Jr. He went to a party at the, you know, Playboy Mansion in 2005 - Playboy Superbowl Party. I don't know if it was actually at the mansion, but it was a Playboy party.
And he said I like football and I like girls. I don't want to apologize. But now there's a Republican National Committee ad condemning his ways. Let's take a listen.

So what kind of man parties with Playboy playmates in lingerie, then films political ads from a church pew? What kind of man is Harold Ford? The National Republican Senatorial Committee is responsible for the content of this ad.

Yvonne, should women be offended? Should men be offended? Should everyone be offended by Harold Ford, or should people be offended by the ad, which has overtones of, you know, misagination - you know, blonde women and talking about Harold? And, you know, there's been a lot of criticism that this might be more of a racial attack than a sexual attack.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: Harold Ford should be ashamed of Harold Ford. At this point throughout his career, he has been very careful in terms of sculpting his image as well as his political message. And to try and at least,appear that he was in the mainstream of the political spectrum, I think that there was no way that he should have not understood the political ramifications of him appearing at a party associated with Playboy.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: Now, as a private citizen, and you know whether or not that's his right, you know, that's his business. But he is not a public - a private citizen, he's running for a high political office. So certainly there are people in the South and in other parts of the country that do buy into the whole racial undertones of seeing some blonde woman talking about Harold Ford. And they can read into it what they will.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: I think that Harold Ford has no one to blame but Harold Ford for whatever comes out of this debacle, and that's it. I mean, I think that in this day and age it's unfortunate. But those feelings - those racial feelings still exists. And he opened a door for his opponent to attack him, rightly or wrongly.
Walter, he made his bed. He's lying in it. It's that how you feel?

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: Not necessarily. I think many Americans are growing to the point that they want to keep politics out of the bedroom. You know, and I think what we're seeing here is the morality play that really isn't working for the Republican Party this election cycle. I'm surprised they used it in Tennessee. That's my shock, given all the skeletons in the GOP closet this year.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: I think it was a strategic mistake to even roll this ad out, because I think it gives Harold Ford - despite what you may think of his personal preferences and choices - I think it gives him another weapon to use against the Republican Party at a time when the state of Tennessee is facing some serious issues.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: This is the best that the Republicans can come up with, that he went to a Playboy party at the Super Bowl. So I think most voters will look at this, including some Republicans, and say you've got to be kidding me. There are more substantive issues to talk about and better things to do of airtime than running an ad like this or the one that runs on TV where you have a blonde sort of winking at him saying call me Harold. I mean it's really juvenile politics at its worst.
Ron, is this a bad ad or is this a strategic and powerful ad?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I don't think it's a bad ad. I agree with what my colleague said earlier. When you run for public office and you put yourself in the public light; if you film political television spots where you're in a church and you hold yourself out to high moral values and high moral character and then you attend a party in Jacksonville, Florida, a Super Bowl party hosted by Playboy magazine; I think that if you're an official in the public light, it allows certain individuals to criticize or to question your morality choices.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: But looking at the broader racial overtones, I think this is a tempest in a teapot and much ado about nothing. To suggest that a blonde woman saying I met Harold Ford at a Playboy party somehow has racial overturns or is racist, which has been so much of the discourse for the last couple of days, I think is ridiculous.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: In my opinion, it is equally racist to suggest that if a particular person who is Caucasian says I met Harold Ford at a party is racist. Are individuals then saying that it should've been an African-American woman saying that or Hispanic woman? I think this is much ado about nothing. But right or wrong, Mr. Ford has put himself in the crosshairs by holding himself up to be a strong moral character, and then attending that party and - at Playboy party - and then allowing his opponents the opportunity to criticize him.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: Farai, can I…
Go ahead.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: I just want to add one thing. I think that's a complete misunderstanding of U.S. history, particularly in the South. The notion of interracial relationships have yet to really receive mainstream support in some of those Southern states. And I think there's a subliminal message that is given. If that were the case, then why not have a black woman in that ad that says call me Harold?

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: That was a decision made by campaign strategists to pitch to a certain segment of the electorate. I suspect white males who are probably more likely to support the Republican candidate because they could've easily chosen a black woman. So I think to suggest that race had nothing to do with the thinking behind that ad is a complete misread of not only current politics but our history. So I don't think you can walk away from the racial factor.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: I would just suggest that given the fact that morality is not going to win the day for the Republican Party, not considering everything that they have on their plate, I think it was a dumb move by the Republicans. I don't think it's going to work for them in Tennessee.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: And I have to just, very briefly, respectfully respond to that in my reading of history. It is - I think your statement, candidly, is a little bit disingenuous. If there are those individuals in Tennessee who are not going to vote for an African-American man for the United States Senate based on a woman in a television spot, I think that's silly. You know (unintelligible) -excuse me -

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: No, based upon a white woman in a television man.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Excuse me.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: Make that distinction.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I'll make…

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: Make that distinction. That was the ad.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Fine. I - fine. I will make the distinction. I'm suggesting, however, that if individuals are racist and not going to vote for African-American man in the United States Senate, I suspect that their minds have already been made up to this point and not based on one single ad with one blonde woman.

All right. We have time for just one more topic. And briefly, Justice Department reached a settlement with Armstrong Williams, the conservative commentator, over his promotion of the Bush administration education reforms. He was not guilty of any criminal violations even though he was paid. Now on the other side, a company headed by President Bush's brother and partly owned by his parents may be benefiting from the No Child Left Behind Law. It's an educational products distribution company.
So these two controversies or these two issues, is No Child Left Behind falling prey to abuse? I'm going to ask you, Yvonne, to start us of.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: Well, I think that the topics are somewhat different. In terms of Armstrong Williams, I think that the main issue as the public viewed it, as a Justice Department viewed it, was that he was holding himself out as a neutral person when in fact he was taking money through I believe a publicity arm that he had formed. And he had not been fully candid with the public in so doing.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: I think the Bush family issue is different from the standpoint. Neil Bush is presenting himself as a businessman, a businessman who is selling educational products. And at this point, some people have signed on. They think it's the greatest thing since sliced bread. Other people have not blood or re-upped their orders because they don't think that that the product is that good. So I'm not sure that I see abuse in the same way in these two particular issues.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: I think Armstrong Williams, he might not have been found guilty of any criminal misconduct, but he wasn't forthright in letting the public know what his associations were when he was making these promotions of No Child Left Behind.
I'm going to have to cut you off.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: Okay.
Unfortunately, very, very quickly, Ron and then Walter.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Armstrong Williams was a case of poor judgment. In full disclosure, he should have let it be known to his listeners, to his client base that in fact he had taken money from the Department of Education and to act as a surrogate or to act for publicity purposes. And I think that the condemnation from the public is well deserved.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: As it relates to Neil Bush and Ignite!, No Child Left Behind gives money to the states to establish curriculum for math and for reading for middle school children, primarily. And I think that those funds are best left to the states to determine which programs, which companies, which deliverers of services are best in a position to fulfill the requirements of No Child Left Behind. So I think there's a distinction. And from what I've been able to save thus far, there's nothing wrong with what Neil Bush has done and what the Bush family has done here.
Walter, quickly.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: I think it's a part of the larger moral and ethical contradiction of Republican conservatives that you stand on morality. And I think they're going to fall on morality. So whether it'd Armstrong Williams or Neil Bush, who, I think the last time we heard from him was in an S&L scandal.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: So, you know, I think part of what we have to look at is that there is a pattern here, and there's even a pattern among black conservatives. I mean you had Clarence Thomas who was nominated to the Supreme Court admitting that he had a collection of erotica, which some of us would just simply call porn. So you have these Republicans who stand on these moral issues. But when you open up the closet, you have to get out of the way because they don't have skeletons - they've got a whole cemetery.

All right. We got to leave it there. I'm sure that they'll be back -folks will be back to listen more. Walter Fields of the Northstarnetwork.com. Ron Christie, Vice president for the D.C. Navigators. And Yvonne Bynoe, author of Stand and Deliver, thank you all.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: Thank you.

speaker_label: Ms. YVONNE BYNOE (Author, Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership in Hip-Hop Culture)
text: Thank you.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Thank you.
Next on NEWS & NOTES, Political Corner: The scandal around Louisiana Congressman William Jefferson. Plus, a journey of love, identity and forgiveness in a new novel called Heat Signature.
You're listening to News & Notes from NPR News.

Now we turn to our Roundtable to talk more about the election. Joining us today from Just(ph) Studios near Detroit, Michigan, is Rochelle Riley, columnist for the Detroit Free Press. We've got Ron Christie, vice president of the D.C. Navigators and former deputy assistant to Vice President Dick Cheney, in our headquarters in Washington, D.C. And in Nashville, Tennessee, at Spotland Productions is Jeff Obafemi Carr, host of the radio show Freestyle.

So welcome, everyone. And let me turn first to what Congressman Rangel said. With a bit of glee, you know, I may not be there in 2010 but the president definitely won't. How much do you think, Ron, that this Congress, this House, will really try to stick it to the president?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Well, it's very interesting. First of all, the American people have spoken last night, and they're very angry with the Republicans. And looking at what has happened over the last night it will be very interesting to hear what politicians from both parties hear.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Will the Democrats hear from the American people that they have a mandate to use the subpoena power to go after the administration and to really become a confrontational party to the Republicans? And also what will the Republicans hear? Will they recognize that their conservative principles that they came into power on were not followed? We had a lot of scandals, so what will they hear?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: But to answer your question most directly, I do believe that Charlie Rangel and many of the other Democrats who will assume the gavels in the House of Representatives will make the president's life very difficult over the next two years.
Jeff, you are in Tennessee. How are people there reading the tea leaves on Harold Ford?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Well, people are trying to now kind of determine what he's going to do. There is a lot of disappointment about what happened with Harold Ford. But it's kind of indicative of what might happen with the Democratic Party in general in terms of finding an identity.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: With the Democratic Party I think the shift of power in D.C. now will play out in how they are able to come together. I think Pat Buchanan on TV early this morning was talking about the different kind of factions that are in the Democratic Party itself.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: And when you think about the campaign that Harold Ford Jr. ran here in Tennessee, it was a strong campaign. For the first time I saw people standing in lines around the block. I saw college students on the corner with signs telling people to vote and vans moving people all around. It was a very galvanizing campaign.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: But at the same time, if you remove the race issue, Ford was saying basically the exact same thing in a policy manner that Corker was. And so there's this notion of the, quote, “blue-dog Democrat,” end quote, that came about as a result of Democrats trying to appeal to the more conservative element of the population of America.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: And to see how that's going to turn around and now bite them is going to be interesting to watch play out.
Rochelle, I understand you've been tracking how women fared. And, you know, certainly Nancy Pelosi is in a position to take power. How have women overall fared in this election?

speaker_label: Ms. ROCHELLE RILEY (Columnist, Detroit Free Press)
text: Well, it was an interesting year for women. Before I want to talk about them, I do want to to your previous question say that one of the more interesting things to watch is whether the Republicans who had just distanced themselves from the president will now be rats running from a sinking ship. I think it's not going to be just Democrats who are going to be making life difficult for President Bush.

speaker_label: Ms. ROCHELLE RILEY (Columnist, Detroit Free Press)
text: But back to women - 140 women were running for the House last night and 12 women running for the Senate. There's already record numbers of women in the House and Senate - 67 in the House and 14 in the Senate. I think that what you're seeing is women stepping up in a way that they have not done since the year of the woman, 1992.

speaker_label: Ms. ROCHELLE RILEY (Columnist, Detroit Free Press)
text: While you can't have those same gains, the same numbers of wins, no matter how many women will win it still will increase that record and will change the face of what's happening, particularly on some committees.

speaker_label: Ms. ROCHELLE RILEY (Columnist, Detroit Free Press)
text: In governor's races, there were 36 governor's races last night and there were 10 women running. And four women were reelected thus far. There are still a couple of races that have yet to be decided.

Ron, I want to touch on George Allen. There's going to be legal challenges in the Allen/Webb race. Voters in the region in Virginia reported suspicious phones calls trying to mislead them before voting, this according to NBC News. You worked for George Allen. You know, what do you make of that race?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I think it is going to go down to the wire. It's going to be extremely tight. I did work for George Allen. I was his deputy policy director during this first bid for the United States Senate back in 2000, and the demographics of the commonwealth of Virginia have really changed.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Six years ago, when he was first running for the Senate, Loudoun County, just a little bit away from Washington, D.C., was a solid Republican area. Now that you look at the outlying areas near Washington, D.C. and Virginia, Loudoun County, some parts of Fairfax County, Prince William Counties, areas where the Republicans consistently thought were their strongholds are now increasingly going to the Democrats.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: So for George Allen to prevail in this very, very narrow contest, he's going to have to have to very well in northern Virginia for some of these recounts and it's going to be extremely, extremely close.

Rochelle, what about the aspect of potential voter intimidation? This is something that really this year a whole bunch of watchdog groups on the left and the right really focused on dealing with immediate legal challenges to voter intimidation. There have been projects like Video the Vote that were videoing at polls.
What can we expect from the Webb/Allen race and from other races in terms of dealing with potential voter intimidation?

speaker_label: Ms. ROCHELLE RILEY (Columnist, Detroit Free Press)
text: Well, I think that a lot of the clerks - the city clerk here in Detroit did several training sessions and worked a lot in advance. But the bottom line is you can't stop it before you see it. And the biggest obstacle that many of these clerks face is getting people to understand that there still is voter intimidation.

speaker_label: Ms. ROCHELLE RILEY (Columnist, Detroit Free Press)
text: There are poll watchers who are getting too close to voters, asking questions a little too loudly. There are people from various parties who are supposed to be checking just to make sure that the information is correct at the same time the poll workers are checking, but they're leaning in a little too far, asking questions directly of voters. And that's intimidating for some older voters who remember days when a question like that could lead to your being sent home or worse.

speaker_label: Ms. ROCHELLE RILEY (Columnist, Detroit Free Press)
text: So it is a real problem. I think that between the problems with the voting machines and with some sense of intimidation we're going to have a smaller repeat of Florida in 2000.

Jeff, you know Governor Mark Sanford of South Carolina couldn't even vote the first time because he didn't have the proper ID. Are we going to resign ourselves to a situation where there's increasing tension between people who are focused on voter intimidation and people who are focused on voter validation and IDs and things like that?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Well, I think so. And I think this whole issue of voter intimidation in the America that we live in is a real concern. Because of all the legal challenges that grew out of, say, the last couple of presidential elections, I felt a little trepidation when I went to the polls.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: The poll watchers, they can be unnerving. In the booth itself we had some extensive resolutions that were oddly worded in a legalese that wasn't easily interpreted. And although there was a touch screen voting machine, there were resolutions that were incomplete as presented there, so there were taped pieces of paper hanging off the inside of the machine that supposedly explained the information.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: The lines were long. It could have been intimidating for a lot of people, and that's just the voting process itself. I can't imagine getting phone calls that could confuse you or thinking about the battery of lawyers that were dispatched in this whole election from both parties and all the watchdog groups that supposedly support the troops in this political war.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: So when we look at it, it's really not quite as easy to vote in the so-called greatest democracy in the world as we think.

Well, speaking of ballot initiatives, you mentioned those. The Michigan Civil Rights Initiative looks like it passed and, you know, 99 percent of the precincts counted, 58 percent of the voters that are counted say all right, let's eliminate affirmative action in public education, employment and contracting.
Now Ward Connerly, who also passed a similar initiative in California, praised the Ku Klux Klan's support of the initiative. Let's take a listen.

The Michigan Civil Rights Initiative is an entity that has not affiliated itself in any way with any mainstream civil rights organizations. In fact, the only entity that's endorsed the MCRI is the Ku Klux Klan.

speaker_label: Mr. WARD CONNERLY (Founder, American Civil Rights Institute)
text: If the Ku Klux Klan thinks that equality is right, God bless them. Thank them for finally reaching the point where logic and reason are applying - are being applied instead of hate.
That was a clip from a documentary. First the narrator's voice and then Ward Connerly's voice.
What can we make of this, Jeff? I mean this passed and should we be focused at all on the Ku Klux Klan issue, or the law itself?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Okay, I'm going to be frank here. You say 58 percent of the people passed this law. I think that probably it will be repealed one day as some of the resolutions in California were that Ward Connerly instituted or worked for.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Now there are people in history that will be looked on as great thinkers, idealists, visionaries on all kind of landscapes - education, politics, et cetera - simply because they advanced ideas that at the time were not very popular or widely accepted, and we could come up with a lot of these people in a laundry list.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Then there are people who are sycophants, who never say anything new, who snatch all kinds of headlines about a simple fact that they have these gimmicky kind of regurgitations of worn-out incendiary philosophies. Ward Connerly is in the latter class but perhaps he has a notion that he's in the former.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: This is not ad homonym, but any cat that makes money on real estate and particularly in affirmative action and then turns around later in his career and would embrace people like the KKK, who would gut him like a scarecrow in The Wiz on any given night in a wooded field, might need to consider getting medication.
Whoa. Ron, what do you think?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Wow. I think that the initiative process has worked across the country and continues to work when people either at the federal level or at the state level fail to enact particular legislation that the people want.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: But looking at Ward Connerly in particular, I found his comments relating to the Klan to be very offensive. The Ku Klux Klan is not an equal rights or an equal opportunity organization. They would kill African Americans, people of the Jewish faith and other individuals based specifically on their religious or their ethnic identity. And to hearken to the Klan for any sort of support for a ballot initiative I think is obscene.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: If the people in Michigan have decided that they want to support a particular initiative, that's fine for the people of Michigan but keep the Klan out of it.
Rochelle, do you think that this will be challenged? And what does it say about America's stance on how to achieve racial equality at this point in time?

speaker_label: Ms. ROCHELLE RILEY (Columnist, Detroit Free Press)
text: Well, not only will it be challenged but it will be challenged numerous times, so millions of dollars that could have gone to other things will have to be spent defending this initiative.

speaker_label: Ms. ROCHELLE RILEY (Columnist, Detroit Free Press)
text: I think part of the problem is the campaign against the initiative tried to make this about Ward Connerly and did not spend enough time talking about why affirmative action existed and the progress that it has helped to create over 30 years. Quite frankly, the Klan comment was not unusual for Ward Connerly, who is indicative of exactly why the phrase exists - a mind is a terrible thing to waste.

speaker_label: Ms. ROCHELLE RILEY (Columnist, Detroit Free Press)
text: I think that what we really needed to do was have some serious discussions about the economics of affirmative action and how it really is helping people who are disadvantaged, disadvantaged in education, disadvantaged with jobs. And in a lot of cases those people happen to be people of color, not just black but Hispanic and in some cases Asian. And I think that what we've done now is thrown the baby out with the bath water without trying to figure out what we're going to do to continue to make some progress.

All right. We're going to have to leave it there, but we look forward to more discussion of this race and looking forward to 2008 already. This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya. On today's Roundtable, Senator Barack Obama calls for a withdrawal from Iraq in 2007, and should men in prison be given condoms?

Joining us from our New York bureau is E.R. Shipp, professor in journalism at Hofstra University's School of Communication. We've also got right here with me in Washington, D.C., Ron Christie, vice president of a lobbying firm D.C. Navigators and former deputy assistant to Vice President Dick Cheney. Welcome everyone, and let me go straight to Barack Obama. The senator said on Monday that U.S. troops should start leaving Iraq in 2007, which, frankly, is not that far away. He argued that conditions in Iraq have worsened as the death toll approaches 2,900.
Now in a speech captured by a Chicago station he said we need to encourage Iraq to use more diplomacy. Let's take a listen.
We must communicate clearly and effectively to the factions in Iraq that the days of asking, urging and waiting for them to take control of their own country are coming to an end.
Ron, you're right here with me in D.C. I can get to travel a little bit these days. Is this just too much to ask too soon?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I think it is too much to ask too soon. The Constitution of the United States provides the Congress with the ability to authorize war, but it gives the president of the United States the ability to wage that war as commander in chief.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I think if you look at a date certain for pullout in 2007, I think that would be extraordinarily dangerous to all the progress that has gone on overseas in Iraq. And if you look at history, Farai, I think one of the things about what Senator Obama had to say that struck me is if you look at World War II and the number of the years and sadly the number of thousands of American soldiers who lost their lives defending their country. If Barack Obama, Senator Obama is looking at 2,900 lives and saying that it's a catastrophic failure and we need to leave, I think it shows a lack of sophistication at looking at the history of the United States and the struggles of winning a very, very difficult war.

E.R., we had on the former U.S. Secretary of the Army Togo West, and he said that basically the U.S. is good at getting into countries, good at fighting, and doesn't always have the best means of getting out. So if that's the case, I mean if you're sort of darned if you, darned if you don't - using my G-rated language - in terms of setting a date for withdrawal?

Professor E.R. SHIPP (Journalism, Hofstra University): Well, first of all, what Obama is saying is not unlike what others are saying, including some military officials. It's not so much that he's saying there needs to be a definite date, say, June 6, 2007, or something. He's saying we need to make 2007 the year that the Iraqis need to step up to the plate as we make determinations that are best for our interest.

This is an interesting thing for Obama to take on right now because so far he's been able to coast on his good looks and the status of the rock star of the Democratic Party. So it would be very interesting now to see, as he's toying with the idea of becoming a presidential candidate, whether he's very serious about taking on a tough issue like the war in Iraq and terrorism.
Jeff, do you think that's really the core of it, that Barack Obama is trying to beef up his foreign policy credentials?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: I think that's definitely a part of it, and I think he's smart for doing so. And I think he's making quite a statement by articulating this issue in the way he's articulating it. Notice that he said 2007, immediately when we think 2007 we think January. But in actuality this could be over a year from now, and without setting that date he kind of opens it up for ideas to come around.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: And he's making a statement in this. He's saying that he's consistent. He said the same thing last year, he's saying it a year later, and he's stating that he hopes he won't be saying the same thing next year. He's very clear. This plan may be the most well balanced articulation of both American popular sentiment and political expediency. And he's making sense in positioning himself very much as a man of the people, so to speak.

Jeff, I'm going to come at you with a different topic. This is one that, you know, it's a tough issue. There are some folks who are pressing to make condoms available in prisons. I mean when you have a situation where, you know, you don't always have HIV testing or adequate drugs, the National Minority AIDS Council made that one of their recommendations.

And, you know, African-Americans are ten-times more likely than white Americans to have AIDS. So is it time to acknowledge that people are having sex in prison with whoever's around and that this is a means of transmission not just between people in prison but also whoever they contact outside of prison.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Yeah, this is a very serious issue. And we can approach it on a lot of different levels. But I also have to think something we have to keep in mind here is a throwback to the movie “The Shawshank Redemption” - everyone in prison is innocent. In this case, no one in prison is homosexual, and that's part of the problem.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: There's this notion that if I have to take a condom, use a condom, then I am stating that I am in fact something that I'm claiming I'm not. It's what has sparked the African-American notion of the down-low phenomenon where people don't want to practice safe sexual behavior because it is a step that makes you acknowledge that you have these same-sex feelings, whether that comes from a desire that's inside or from a survival mentality when we talk about the prison population.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: I think definitely making condoms available there and acknowledging that this behavior is happening is a step. But it's also another step to get people to actually use those. Ninety-five percent of the prisons out there aren't even issuing the condoms. But it's just sad that out of 1.1 million HIV cases almost half of them are black in a country where we only make up 13 percent of the U.S. population. That's astounding to me and something definitely has to be done.

E.R., it strikes me that, you know, there's been all these new language around the issue of what some people call the down low like MSM, men having sex with men. So, okay, we're not going to call them gay. We're not going to say that they are having gay sex. We're going to say that they are men having sex with men.

Add to that another layer, which is that of course in prison rape is part of the sexual behavior. I'm sure it's not all of it. It's definitely not all of it, but part of it is forced. Even if you had the condoms in the prisons, would it make a difference, do you think?

Well, on this issue, I have to start this: I'm not a prude exactly, but I'm opposed to issuing condoms in prison. It would be acknowledging and actually enabling perhaps this kind of misbehavior, sex going on, whether it's forced or not. So I'm against this.

There are serious issues in the black community about how to deal with AIDS and there are serious issues about this whole down low, men having sex with men phenomenon. I think the way to address that is through education and prevention focused on the people in the civilian population, not in the prison population at this stage.
But they're mixing. You know, once you have people through the revolving door, you have people…
Well, once they're on the outside…
…people who might have a girlfriend on the outside. They go outside -

Well, girlfriend needs to make sure boyfriend has a condom. But on the outside I think there are more opportunities for these organizations such as those who got together earlier this year to sign a declaration of commitment to end AIDS epidemic in black America, that included civil rights organizations, media companies, churches, et cetera.
I think there are more opportunities to address the issue on the outside than to condone this misbehavior in prison by distributing condoms.
Ron, if this saves even one life, isn't it worth it? I mean…

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Well, I actually agree with most of what E.R. had to say. Certainly, I think that our prison officials are trying to save lives and to make prison, a very difficult situation, as safe as possible.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I discussed this with my wife who is a federal probation officer for almost eight years, and she said that for many years there was not an acknowledgement that either homosexual activity was taking place in the prisons or that there were rapes that were taking place.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Now I think that this discussion is out on the table and folks are talking about it. This report discusses it in great length. But what my wife said that I agree with is that the money that would be spent for condoms should be better used for, one, looking at HIV tests when inmates are coming into prisons so that we can segregate people who already have the HIV strain once they arrive in the prison system.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: And two, that money could also be utilized for better surveillance and in increasing the salary of the prison guards so that we can cut down - again, having sex in prison is not a right. Inmates are not allowed to drink alcohol. They are not allowed to smoke cigarettes to the best extent possible.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Why don't we utilize these funds so that we can have better surveillance and to test people for HIV and look at different ways to cut down on that disease transmission in prison.

But if you segregate the HIV-positive population that could have other ramifications. I mean, for one, you could have a stigma of like cell block whatever that, you know, all those are where the AIDS guys are and you might get into some, you know, equal rights issues if people are not vigilant about being, you know, good stewards of those people. And then, believe it or not, from what I understand, people with HIV can be re-infected with different strains.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Correct.
So, if there's sex there then - I'm just bringing up, I mean there's no easy answer here. But I mean do you…

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: That's right. There's no easy answer. But I do think that we need to take more steps when inmates are being processed to ascertain what the extent of the problem is. It's that we discussed at the top of the segment. For goodness' sakes, 13 percent of the American population is African-American but 40 percent of our prison population is African-American. We need to take solid steps. I think this report is forcing us to have a debate and have a discussion, and that's what we should be doing.
All right.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: And we'd also…
Go ahead, Jeff.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: I was just going to chime in, Farai, that, you know, we quote the statistics on one end but we don't quote them on the other. Statistically, our population is being re-infected by people who are coming out of prisons with the notions that there's a shortage of black men. Women are now interacting more with people who go in and out of the jails.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: And I've discussed this issue with actual prisoners when I actually go and visit and talk with people in prison. And there's a process of survival that goes on there where these people, where people who are in jail and lock down, they do what they feel they need to do to survive.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Sometimes it happens with rape. Sometimes it's a survivalist mentality. I'm just going to do this while I'm here. And there is such shame associated with it that they don't talk about it. So the fact is our women, especially black women, are being infected with HIV. And if we pretend they don't exist or don't try to find ways to at least keep that transmission from taking place in the prison, then we're just going to see our population decimated.

But that brings it back to the responsibility of the women who are going to be in the lives of these men in an intimate way to take more responsibility, too. We've had a discussion on this issue of older women in particular being infected with HIV because in part they are embarrassed to ask their companions to use condoms. They need to take that step. You have to do that.

It sounds like a lot of responsibility and a lot of thought's going to have to go in all around. Final topic, happiness - after we've been talking about something so heavy - are people in countries that are developing happier than people in the developed world?

In the U.S. and Britain, less than 30 percent of people ages 16 to 34 were happy with the way things were maybe because we had been told too many times that we don't have the right thighs, we don't have the right hair. On the contrary, in Argentina and South Africa, 75 percent of young people claim to be happy. E.R. what's up with that?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I don't know. It sort of sounds like the old adage ignorance is bliss; now we're saying, you know ignorance of life beyond your world makes you happy. I think that…
But do we really think that - I mean I think that South Africans are not ignorant of what's beyond their world…
No.
In my impression, having been there.

Well, in some ways, though, when we're lumping all these countries together it's kind of hard to make generalizations. But it seems to me that what this is saying is that the less exposure you have to the endless possibilities of life, the happier you may be.

We, in this very materialistic society in which we live, are always tempted by all kinds of things, from fancy cars to fancy clothes to whatever. And we would probably, our guess, tend to be less happy if we are not able to attain those things. If you're in a country where that's even not a consideration, you don't have those worries. And so a happiness poll may show you to be more happy than we are.

Well, you know, Ron, the least happy place for young people is Japan, of all places. I have been there and there's - it's kind of like the youth wonderland. There's just so many stores and shopping and gadgets, and that would kind of track with what E.R. was saying - that if the more you see, the less comfortable you are. Does that kind of cut against what we think of the American dream, which is that the American dream is about acquiring a better life. But it sounds like a better life is maybe a smaller life.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I think you're right. I think the pressure today on so many of our young children is to gain as much wealth to look like the picture-perfect model and to achieve these materialistic assets. And that puts a lot of pressure on people, and you have to go to the right school and you have to go the right college, and you have to be wearing the right clothes.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Whereas if perhaps - and again I'm just generalizing - if you're in a situation where you're in a developing nation or you spend a lot more time bonding with your family and surviving and slowly moving up the strata, I think that your happiness is derived on your interactions with your loved ones and your families; as opposed to in the States and Japan and Britain and so many of these other countries where so much pressure is placed on our young children, and young girls in particular, of looking the right way or dressing the right way or being a certain way. And if you don't fit in, oh my goodness, what amount of pressure that puts on you.

Jeff, I wonder, you know, and I'm not sure about this, how does this effects African-American youth in particular, because if you look at the incomes of black folks, overall it's lower. But the materialism, the bling factor in terms of what you see on MTV or BET or, you know, VH1, the bling factor is outrageous. So how does this affect, you know, black youth?

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Well, it will affect us more because we have different things that we strive for. So we want the bling. And even if we're in impoverished communities, there's always the story of the one in a million kid who, through athletics or through rapping, made it to the bling level. So we all aspire to that. Our kids aspire to that.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: My daughter, I can send her outside and she can say in five minutes I'm bored. And I can't imagine that. And I think the reason why these more developed countries have promises that they - in a lower developed countries, they're happier because they have fewer Sony PSPs to have taken away from them.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: And I think of my childhood before the laptop and Internet and movie and MTV and gaming addictions, we used to make bottle-cap guns and build forts out of scrap wood, and we just had make-up play lives. We were very, very happy with whatever was around us, creating things. So perhaps this study reinforces that age-old adage that the best things in life are indeed free.
All right, E.R., we're almost out of time, but any final thoughts on how maybe we can reverse the trend?

Well, I think what we need to do is to focus more on family ties and community ties. And to make that the focus of our young people's lives as opposed to the kind of activities we've seen in the last week where everybody was trying to get these new PlayStations and Nintendos.
And sometimes getting shot trying to do it.
Yes, having fights and riots and all of that.

All right. We're going to have to leave it there. E.R. Shipp of Hofstra University School of Communication; Ron Christie, vice president of D.C. Navigators; and Jeff Obafemi Carr of the radio show “Freestyle.” Remember to start cooking early, because folks going to be coming over to your house. Thank you all.
I got a nice turkey.

speaker_label: Mr. JEFF OBAFEMI CARR (Radio Host, Freestyle)
text: Happy thanksgiving.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Thank you, Farai.

On today's Roundtable, U.S. deaths in Iraq crossed the 3,000 mark, but what about casualties? And a new year means new laws.

Joining us today is Michael Meyers, executive director of the New York Civil Rights Coalition; Laura Washington, Chicago Sun-Times columnist in Chicago; and Ron Christie, vice president of the lobbying firm D.C. Navigators and former deputy assistant to Vice President Dick Cheney.
Thank you all for being with us.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Same here.

So let's talk a little bit about this issue of the casualties. You know, the deaths of U.S. military personnel sadly crossed the 3,000 mark over the New Year. But NPR is also reporting that casualties, seriously wounded troops in the conflict, are at the 22,000 level. And military experts have said, you know, casualties are actually more important to count than deaths; because of people wearing body armor, people come back without the function of several limbs but they are able to survive.

So Ron, is it important for us to really take a look at a bigger picture? Because the deaths from Vietnam, for example, were many, many times what U.S. troop deaths have been so far, but the casualties are really up there much higher than we thought?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Well, it's a tragedy. There's no question about it. On September 11th, 2001, nearly 3,000 innocent Americans lost their lives as they went about their everyday activities.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: As a result to that the United States went to war, and unfortunately our military men and women have lost their lives, nearly 3,000, and the casualty figures, you've pointed out, is over 20,000. Every casualty is a terrible tragedy, but these brave men and women who put on the uniform are trying to protect this country, trying to ensure that we don't have another terrorist attack and trying to preserve our way of life. And they understand the risks and they understand that they could be seriously injured or that they could ultimately pay the ultimate sacrifice with their own lives.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: But we need to do everything that we can, Farai, once they return home, to do the proper rehabilitation and to really assimilate them back in society. And it's our incumbent responsibility to take care of these brave men and women who are taking care of us.

Laura, you know, I was struck when over the holidays I went to the beach, which is something you can do on Christmas Day with your family, which is what I did. We went to the beach in Santa Monica. We were on the pier, and we looked out over the pier and there was an exhibition of crosses. Each one individually named for a dead American troop member.

And it was really amazing to me that you could see that there has been some kind of psychological turning point where people across the country are at different times putting up these huge memorials to the troops who've died. And I wonder if the troops who have been seriously wounded feel as if they are counted as much in the equation of what we have gained and what we have lost.

Well, Farai, I think the reason that you see for the crosses is I think, among many military families -I think among many Americans there is much frustration about what many people feel is the lack of acknowledgement or full acknowledgement of the casualties and the impact the Bush administration has played down.

Obviously, Bush is always very consoling to families, but they have played down the actual casualties. They don't want you to see the bodies. They don't want you to see the coffins. So I think that this is a response to that. I think that the issue of casualties has some recent in technology because we have become much better at treating wounds; there's things like making sure that the troops have tourniquets when they are on the ground, when they are out in the field, to make sure that there are more sophisticated care techniques. And I - and also the fact that the bombs have become so much more sophisticated.

I think all of these things - in some ways, it's a double edged sword. In some ways, we've been able to save more lives. We've been able to get to catch more people before it gets to the wounds get too serious. But on the other hand, these devices, these IEDs, are very, very dangerous and they cause these irreparable injuries.

And I think, you know, when you talk about Agent Orange and what happened to the Vietnam class. The kind of impact we're going to be seeing in 5, 10, 20 years out in terms of these people coming home and needing to be cared for and not being able to be full members of society because of their sacrifice, I think it's going to haunt us for decades to come.

Michael, what about that? Are we prepared as a nation to really extend generosity to people who have made, if not the ultimate sacrifice, sacrificed a limb, sacrificed due to a brain injury? Are we prepared to really deal with a generation of people who may have a lot of limitations physically and sometimes mentally because of the war?

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Well, based on our recent history, there is no evidence of it. There's just no evidence of it. Vietnam War veterans will attest to that. And I don't know what Ron is talking about; there's no evidence of a connection between the 3,000 who are dead because of the attacks on America and the World Trade Center and in the air, that there was any connection with Iraq. Like there's no evidence of weapons of mass destruction that were held by Iraq. No evidence, Ron. This is a policy of war…

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Well, I actually -

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: Excuse me. Excuse me. When you have a policy of war, we're in and on a death count. And when you have a policy of war, you're in and you're on a casualty count and you can't get away from that. For me, this issue is not 3,000, not 4,000, not 5,000 more deaths, not 22,000 casualties or 5,000 casualties; for me, the question is when do we get out of Iraq.

speaker_label: Mr. MICHAEL MEYERS (Executive Director, New York Civil Rights Coalition)
text: And the president is buying more time and talking about putting more troops in even after the elections which said to him, stop it, get out of there.

Ron, before I let you jump in, I want a transition to Saddam Hussein. I mean Michael is just arguing about the issue of weapons of mass destruction. speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: So, I think that we have to maintain a check and balance in our government. speaker_label: Professor MARCELO SUAREZ-OROZCO (Education and Globalization, New York University)
text: What I would propose is that to have Attorney General Al Gonzales to issue a finding on this…
I like that.

speaker_label: Professor MARCELO SUAREZ-OROZCO (Education and Globalization, New York University)
text: …matter of a serious concern to our democracy.

Well, you know, Ron, I'll leave it with you. I realize this is a very different topic than the other ones we've been talking about. But, you know, there is still a need in television to have multi-racial shows. And isn't it a shame on some level that this behind-the-scenes drama is taking away from the success of a multiracial show with an African-American woman who leads it?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I think that's true. "Grey's Anatomy" is one of my favorite TV shows, and it does have a very diverse and a very rich cast. And they should leave the drama to the set and keep their own personal opinions and their personal thoughts to themselves. And I agree with Yvonne. We don't know what happened. It was a he said, she said incident on the set of the show, and none of us were there and know what happened.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: But it seems to me that these people need to be cognizant of the fact that they're very highly paid, that they are role models to many in our community, and that they need to grow up and get over it and get along.

We will leave it there. Yvonne Bynoe, author of the book "Stand and Deliver: Political Activism Leadership and Hip-hop Culture," Ron Christie, vice president of the lobbying firm DC Navigators, former deputy assistant to Vice President Dick Cheney, and Marcelo Suarez-Orozco, professor of education and globalization at New York University - who may also have a line to Alberto Gonzales.
Ask him what he thinks about television drama. Thank you all so much.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Nice to be with you.
