From NPR News, this is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Tony Cox in for Farai Chideya, who is on vacation.

Last night, President Bush delivered his 7th annual address to the nation and it was perhaps one of the toughest speeches of his political career. Public support for the Iraq war is low and for the first time he faced a Democratic majority in the House chamber. The president continued to defend his Iraq strategy but he also outlined a domestic agenda for the new year with a collection of policies, old and new.

For a closer look at his remarks, we are joined now from the studios of Princeton University by Melissa Harris-Lacewell, associate professor of politics and African-American studies, and from NPR's Washington D.C. headquarters, Ron Christie, vice president of the lobbying firm D.C. Navigators. He is also former special assistant to President George W. Bush.
Melissa, Ron, nice to have both of you on.

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: Thanks for having me.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: It's nice to join you today.

Before we get into the specifics of the president's speech, let's start with both of your general impressions. The president did, after all, have a lot of hearts and minds to win last night. So starting with you, Melissa, good speech, so-so speech, well delivered, what do you say?

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: Honestly, as I finally turned off the television kind of late last night, I thought what is this feeling I'm having? And I realized it was a bit like listening to an abusive husband who keeps coming back and telling you that this will be the last time that he'll do something awful. And there comes a point where you just don't believe it anymore.
What do you say, Ron?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I don't know what speech your good professor was listening to. I thought the president took the rostrum last night under very difficult circumstances, delivered a very well-written, very well-crafted set of remarks. And I think he extended the proper olive branch to the Democrat Party and recognized that we're a divided government and that we all need to work together and to find solutions not on this side or that side of the aisle, but we need to cross the aisle to find ways that we can advance the American people's agenda. I thought it was very well done.

All right, let's delve into some of the issues that the president brought up. He not only had to convince the majority of Americans and Democrats that they should tough it out in Iraq, he had to convince many in his own party as well.

President GEORGE W. BUSH: This is not the fight we entered in Iraq, but it is the fight we're in. Every one of us wishes this war were over and won. Yet it would not be like us to leave our promises unkept, our friends abandoned and our own security at risk.
Ladies and gentlemen, on this day, at this hour, it is still within our power to shape the outcome of this battle. Let us find our resolve and turn events toward victory.
So Melissa, given your earlier remarks, is it fair to say you don't feel that he hit the mark with that?

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: Well again, I think we have to keep asking ourselves, so what exactly is this victory that this president is asking us to imagine? See, the goal has been moving so much in this war. First this question of weapons of mass destruction, then this dialogue about the danger of Saddam Hussein, then this notion about building democracy.

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: So since the target keeps moving and each time what the president tells us -that there are weapons of mass destruction - turns out to be untrue. That the world and Iraq will be safer when Saddam Hussein is gone turns out to be untrue. That it's very difficult then to listen to this language about we must keep our promises when we can't even be clear what those promises are, given the moving target.

But one of the things, Ron, that happened in terms of Democratic responses to the president's speech last night with regard to the war in Iraq, from what I was able to discern, is that they weren't necessarily moved. Do you think that some of the Republicans who had questions about Iraq were moved as a result of what the president said?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I think in the opening piece from Senator Norm Coleman last night in Statuary Hall where he said that, you know, the president had a tough road to hoe and that Senator Coleman was optimistic, a little bit more moved perhaps by the president's words last night. But there's no question, Tony, that people on either side of the political spectrum are very concerned, as we all are as Americans, of what's going on in Iraq.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: But let me just rebut something the professor said a second ago. The United States is involved in Iraq to win not just because it's a moving goal post or there were weapons of mass destruction or not weapons of mass destruction. The terrorists themselves have said that they want to fight the infidel - meaning us, the United States - in Iraq. And as our general over there, Abizaid, has said, if we do not take the terrorists over there, the terrorists will come here.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: That is what this struggle - that is what this fight is all about of taking these terrorists out before they inflict more damage on our soil as we've seen from 9/11.

Let's move on to another topic that the president raised last night. It had to do with healthcare and sort of combining healthcare reform and tax reform. He has used simplicity in the past to sell his agenda. But is the idea of rewriting the tax code to pay for healthcare just a little too complicated? Listen to this.

And for the millions of other Americans who have no health insurance at all, this deduction would help put a basic private health insurance plan within their reach. Changing the tax code is a vital and necessary step to making healthcare affordable for more Americans.
Did that message land, Melissa?

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: I'm not completely sure if the message landed in terms of the actual specific policy. He's going to have to do a lot more work. But what I will say landed is that this is what is better about divided government than a government where a single party controls both chambers of Congress and the White House.

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: This president is now forced to at least offer possibilities for addressing these very serious questions around healthcare. I don't think there is one easy, obvious answer. If there was, we would've already taken that up. So I appreciate that there is at least now a proposal from the White House, which will have to be vetted, discussed and clearly changed and updated in the context of not only this legislative session but as we move into the next presidential election.

It seems, Ron, to me that there was some attempt on the part of the president to at least acknowledge and address the bipartisanship that will be necessary to move forward with an agenda that includes things like tax reform and healthcare reform.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I think you're absolutely right, and the president actually said that from the opening moments of the State of the Union last night. Again, that the American people don't care what side of the aisle we sit on; the American people expect us to cross that aisle to work together to find viable solutions to the problems that face us. And healthcare is just one of those problems.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: If you look at the president's proposal, the top fifth of Americans will actually pay a little bit more, but middle-class Americans, lower-class Americans, will receive tax cuts, will have tax deductions. And I think as Melissa said, this is something that will go to the Congress where we'll have a fair debate and fair discussion to find a way to address the 44 to 46 million people in this country without health insurance.
Here's another issue that he addressed: immigration. The one issue that may have played better to this year's crowd than last year's. He renewed his call for a guest worker program.
We need to uphold the great tradition of the melting pot that welcomes and assimilates new arrivals.
We need to resolve the status of the illegal immigrants who are already in our country without animosity and without amnesty.

I was trying to watch Nancy Pelosi last night, Melissa, to get a signal as to which things the president said that she was telling the people in the audience it's OK to clap for this. And immigration was one that I got the sense that maybe this is one they can work together on.

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: Well, absolutely. Not only can they; they're going to have to. And also remember Pelosi is, although speaker of the House, also representative from the State of California, where immigration has been sort of a leading issue even before it hit the complete national stage. So, in fact, if you watch not only Pelosi but some of the Republicans who were in the audience last night, there was a kind of pinched or grimaced look on many of their faces around this language of the president's immigration policy.

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: But this president has been trying to pass this immigration policy for quite some time. It is possible that in this new Congress there will be the possibility of a guest worker program.

Ron, let me beg your indulgence and not ask you to respond on this particular issue because I want to play another piece of tape before we run out of time and I'd like to get your response to that. And it's from Virginia Senator Jim Webb, who struck an unusually blunt tone, it seems, in his response to the president's State of the Union.

These presidents took the right kind of action for the benefit of the American people and for the health of our relations around the world. Tonight, we're calling on this president to take similar action in both areas. If he does, we will join him. If he does not, we will be showing him the way.
Now he was referring to the president's remarks regarding the war, on one hand, and the economy on the other. Those were pretty strong words, were they not?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: They were, and it's an unfortunate choice of language. Senator Webb has shown a lack of maturity and candidly a lack of decorum. He snapped at the president in an event right around the holiday season where he refused to shake his hand and refused to talk about his son when the president asked how his son, Senator Webb's son, who is a Marine overseas in combat in Iraq.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I think the way forward that we all recognize with, particularly with the divided Congress right now, is for people to put aside their personal differences and find ways to work together. And I thought that that response by Senator Webb for the Democrat response was more of the same of partisan and if President Bush is for it then we're against it, which was an unfortunate tone for him to take.
Melissa, it did seem ominous-sounding, didn't it?

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: It was a little ominous. But, I mean, I'm going to cut a little bit of slack for two reasons. One, really the base of the Democratic Party has been calling on the leadership of the Democratic Party to have a backbone. And so part of why they put Webb there is to provide that backbone, to provide that basis to say look, you know, as this president once said, we've got political capital and we're going to spend it.

I don't want to oversimplify the president's speech last night or in any way make it seem less than what it was, but I'd like to ask the both of you as we bring this to a close: On a scale of one to 10, as far as State of the Union speech go that the president has given, this is number seven, what would you give it, Ron?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I give it a seven - strong delivery, strong content and the right tone at the right time.
And Melissa?

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: No, I'd give it much closer to a three or a four. Ultimately, the war in Iraq was overshadowing all of these issues of domestic policy. He really no longer has a bold or a visionary - Whether you disagreed with that vision or not, at least there was a time when he was bold. Now, he really is just that duck.

I appreciate both of you. Melissa Harris-Lacewell is associate professor of politics and African-American studies at Princeton University and the author of "Barbershops, Bibles, and BET." Ron Christie is vice president of the lobbying firm D.C. Navigators. He is also the author of "Black in the White House," and former special assistant to President George W. Bush. Again, thank you both.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Nice to join you.

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: Thank you.

speaker_label: Professor MELISSA HARRIS-LACEWELL (Politics and African-American Studies, Princeton University)
text: Just ahead, the U.S. isn't looking so good in the world's eyes, and hip-hop travels the world for the U.S. State Department.
This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Tony Cox in for Farai Chideya.

On today's Roundtable, America's mayor wants to be America's next president. Fallout from an alleged cover-up shakes the Pentagon. And don't call me articulate. Why that's such a buzzword for black folks.

Joining us to take on these topics on today's Roundtable are E.R. Shipp, professor in journalism at Hofstra University School of Communication, we also have Jeff Obafemi-Carr, and Ron Christie, VP of the lobbying firm DC Navigators and former special assistant to President George W. Bush. Hello, everybody.
Hey, Tony.

Listen. We have a number of topics to get through today, so I'm going to try to push the agenda a little quicker than we normally do. But I'd like to have a brief discussion with you, really briefly, about what we've just heard in our opening segment from the two young African-Americans who are living with HIV. E.R., I suppose the question is how we can expect young people to raise their consciousness about HIV/AIDS when a lot of adults don't.

Professor E.R. SHIPP (Journalism, Hofstra University): That's very true, but I think things are changing sufficiently. Last summer, there was the launch of a new campaign, an awareness campaign. Civil rights organizations, major churches, BET, and others in the communications field decided to get involved in a call for action. And they all pledged that they were going to get the word out to young people as well as to adults.

One of the alarming statistics we're seeing these days is that HIV/AIDS is growing very fast among older black women, many of whom are ashamed to ask their partners to wrap it up, as the young people are saying. And then they are ashamed when they become infected.
Well, what do you think, Jeff, it will take to drive the message home?

I think it's going to take people thinking about this disease on a whole new level and how it really affects, effects and infects people that they know. I was talking once to a person who was talking about the transition in the age gap between the civil rights movement and the current generation and how people tend to blame the kids for ignorance. And he was saying it was like we were great guitar players but we weren't the greatest teachers, so people suffer.

So I think now people in positions of leadership now have to become great teachers. So preachers who are used to speaking to people now have to become good teachers. They have to shirk the shame and start talking about issues that I know are uncomfortable. The same thing with educators, the same thing with people who just interact with people on an everyday basis. We had to really let people know that this is an epidemic space.

And when E.R. mentioned black women especially, you're talking about 25 years old to 34 in their child-bearing age, we have to get rid of the shame that makes us not want to talk about this disease because just because we don't believe it's there doesn't mean that it is.

Well, let me move on to the next topic. And Ron, I'm going to come to you. I apologize for not giving you a chance to chime in on this but I want to come to you when we talk about Rudy Giuliani, the former mayor of New York, filing a so-called statement of candidacy with the Federal Election Commission, making him eligible to raise money for a presidential campaign. Here he is.

speaker_label: Mr. RUDY GIULIANI (Former Mayor of New York City)
text: It is not just about ideologies, it isn't about political parties, it's about who can do it better for our city, our state, and our country.

So one of the questions I have for you, Ron, is this: Can America's mayor, as he is affectionately known, become the GOP front runner despite his stances on abortion, stem cell research, et cetera? Early polls seem to say yes, but maybe.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: I think he can be. I think he's entering into this race is a very important dynamic for the Republican Party. For so much of the commentary that you hear in the airwaves, you hear, oh well, if you're not pro-life and if you're not in certain - if you look at social litmus tests, if you will - if you don't vote the right way or believe the right way in certain issues that you'll never make it pass the early primary stage and then thus not get the nomination.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: I think with Rudy Giuliani what you see here is a dynamic individual, a former U.S. prosecutor who cleaned up New York City when he was the mayor of the city of New York, and someone who a lot of people have a lot of respect for for his leadership and his ability on 9/11. So I do think he can win. It will be incumbent for Giuliani to make a strong impression in the Iowa caucus and the New Hampshire primary. But absolutely I think he has the ability to raise the money. I think he has the stature and ultimately, should Senator Clinton become the Democratic nominee, he has the wherewithal to take her on in a head-to-head in general election.
E.R., would you contrast for us, if you don't mind, his candidacy, the candidacy of Giuliani with that of, let's say, Barack Obama.

That's an interesting contrast. Obama is a fresh face on the scene, so he doesn't have the kind of baggage that Giuliani has. And I say that, I know you introduced the topic of by saying that Giuliani was America's mayor. Well, if you knew Rudy the way we in New York knew Rudy before September 11, you would note that there are a lot of complicated issues there with him. He was not always sensitive to the rights of people, civil liberties. He was not sensitive to blacks and Latinos or poor people. He was not a very nice guy, didn't have a great temperament.

So I think in all of those rough edges Obama has him beat. When it comes to fundraising, he still may be able to trade upon that America's mayor saying until people do get to know Rudy the way we know Rudy.

You know, one of the things, Jeff, that I was thinking about as I pondered the candidacy of Rudy Giuliani as well as that of Barack Obama is the issue of their foreign policy. And how would you characterize - and perhaps it's too early to be able to characterize - the kind of foreign policy stance that will, you know, characterize Giuliani's candidacy?

Well, one of the things that you have to look at is what stage people are used to debating these issues on. Barack Obama and other national figures, even John McCain, are used to at least debating the concept of how to relate to other countries in a position of power to affect those countries, to affect foreign policy.

Giuliani of course as mayor of a very diverse city of course does not have the opportunity or the experience to actually have to interact with other countries. And of course I need to point out that that term America's mayor is like the term America's team, it's a marketing term more than anything. There - it depends on who you ask. There are some people who said, hey, he's not my mayor, especially when you're talking about certain populations that are underserved in New York City.

So on some cases I think Giuliani just - he's a strong candidate. He's very articulate, so to speak. And he articulates a lot of the angst of America, but I think he might be the best thing to happen to the Democratic Party simply because of some of his liabilities in the long term, some of his history with women, and some of his strength that is unwavering and unbending that I don't think you need in an elder statesman of the United States.

Well, certainly his entry into the race will ramp things up. We'll keep our eye on that. We're going to move on to another topic. But before we do, let me just say, if you are listening and just joining us on NEWS & NOTES, I'm Tony Cox. And with me on today's Roundtable are E.R. Shipp, professor in journalism at Hofstra University School of Communication, Jeff Obafemi-Carr, who you just heard, host of the radio show "Freestyle" - he's in Nashville, Tennessee - and also Ron Christie, VP of the lobbying firm DC Navigators. He is the author of "Black in the White House" and former special assistant to President George W. Bush.

speaker_label: All right, moving on to our next topic
text: friendly fire. A video was recently leaked to the media revealing the reaction of an American pilot, pilots actually, after U.S. troops killed a British soldier during a friendly fire incident in Iraq in the early stages of the war. Lance Corporal Matty Hull died when soldiers fired on his convoy nearly four years ago.

speaker_label: All right, moving on to our next topic
text: First it was said that there was no video, but now the Pentagon just says that they won't release it. But of course it's too late. Here's my question. I'm going to come to you, E.R., first. How do you temper situations like these? I mean what obligation, if any, does the Pentagon have here?

Well, I think the Pentagon's position is that it was holding on to the tape as part of its investigation. Anytime there's friendly fire it's a tragedy. It's clearly the allies did not mean to shoot upon each other. So the thing to do is to learn from the error. What went wrong?
Now often what the problem is is not so much the friendly fire incident, but the actions of perhaps cover-up or what appears to be cover-up. And I think that's still being debated in this situation.

Yes, it is, as a matter of fact. And there have been other so-called cover-ups in this war on terror. One of the most recognized was that of former NFL player-turned Army Ranger Pat Tillman. Ron Christie, what do you think the obligation of the administration is with regard to this incident and how it is being handled from this point forward?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: I think as E.R. has just said, every time that you go to battle and every time there is a friendly fire accident, it's a tragedy, and it's a terrible loss of life. And Tony, you just mentioned what happened with Pat Tillman again, another terrible tragedy and loss of life.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: I think the Pentagon and the military officials have an obligation to fully investigate not only what happened at the time of the friendly fire accident, but what has happened in the subsequent years after that initial accident. Was there a cover up? Was there an attempt to deceive, or was that material classified for reasons to protect either troops on the ground or localities or other means or disseminations of intelligence that you don't want those who are our enemies to have.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: So it's important, I think, for the United States government to be fully conversant with their British allies about what happened and it to be transparent but at the same time, we don't want to give our enemies information that's classified or sensitive, should that be that case.
Well, that is the question, isn't it, Jeff, how much information is appropriate to be made public?

Well, of course, and that is and just like Ron said you do have to have some kind of investigation here. But I think that because of the kind of cloak and dagger energy that has surrounded this entire conflict from the beginning. I mean look at the cover up with weapons of mass destruction in the first place and whether or not they existed. I think that the larger question needs to be in investigating issues like this: Is there a system in place that operates with covering up as part of the system itself.
Mm-hmm.

So to what extent do we put things in the column or does the military put things in the column of national security, and people like the family of the person who was killed have no way to redress or to even understand what actually happened. So I think there has to be a balance in there to.
Well, let's move on to our last topic of the day. And let me just say to all three of you, you are so articulate.
Click(ph), click.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: Yeah. Thank you, Tony.
Now, we know that that compliment got Joe Biden in hot water last week. But let's talk about why. Why that's such a big deal? And all of us have heard that. I know.
Yeah.
E.R., what's the big deal?

Well, the big deal is that is that it's not so much calling someone articulate, because on one level it is somehow giving praise -sometimes faint praise. But it's often used inappropriately because where they would say that I am articulate or you are, they might not use the same word to describe a white person. So it becomes one of those phrases that has a subtext to it. They're saying wow, black people know how to string some words together and make sense, and that's the part that's offensive.

Well, you know, Jeff, Jeff Carr, I know that even in my own family, you know, my elders who are from the south. They were like, boy, you're so articulate. We're so proud of you ya-di-ya-di-ya-da - and that was of sense and a source of pride. And yet when it comes from other people, you know there are suspicions attached to it. You know what I mean?

Yeah. There are and I used the term articulate a lot when I'm speaking to three and four-year-olds who amazed me with their ability to use really large word and string them together in a sentence. So for me, I think that that's great because I'm amazed that they are so articulate beyond their years. And when I'm sitting on a panel, and I'm from the south even, so it's interesting because I get this a lot down here.

When you - I'm sitting on a panel with four white people or four white guys, and it's been a great panel. And literally, I've seen people walked by the three white guys and say oh, that was fabulous, I really enjoyed it, and they looked at me and say: you are so articulate.

And to me, when you - and we all know what that means. It's the amazement in their - which psychologically says I have extremely low expectations for you. So you are not the norm, you are the exception. And to me, I personally say this sometimes. I go up and if the white guys been really good, I'd say man, you are really articulate - and they looked kind of shocked.

Well, you know, to be fair, we don't have anybody who's white on the panel today. So I don't really know what's in their heart when they say this. And I would imagine that there are some white people listening to us right now who are saying you know, you all need to get over it. If somebody says you are articulate, just be glad they gave you a compliment and move on. What about that, Ron Christie?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: That's absolutely just so, so wrong, Tony. And I think as the two previous panelists just said, it's almost like they are saying you're so articulate, dot-dot-dot, for a person of color, you know. And I got that in the White House, you know, you would go out and you would represent the administration and you would give a speech and people would say gosh, you know, you're so articulate. You're so well spoken and I'd look at them and say well, I'm a lawyer. You know, I've been to college.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: I mean what would you expect? Do you expect to come up and, I mean, what are you looking for? And so I think as all three of us have articulated, all four of us really, Senator Biden probably got himself on a little bit of hot water by saying these remarks about Senator Obama.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: I'm sure his intentions were pure but we need to recognize that African-Americans have done so much for this country and have contributed so much to this country that to look and refer to us as articulate or well-spoken can be an insult when put in a context of articulate as oppose to what.
You know, it's interesting that you put it that way because this is what I would call a cultural and linguistic divide. My question is: How can we bridge this and move on? And can we do that, Jeff?
How can we do it?
Yeah.

You know it's tough. I mean I think it comes down to - just like when we have conversations about the whole topic of white privilege and whether it still exists. And regardless of what foundation have declared, race is very much still a factor in America. And I think the biggest thing is being able to acknowledge that and listen to it.

It's like a man with a girlfriend and it's the traditional kind of problem as the girl - you talked and the girlfriend's talking and you don't listen, and she says you never listen to me. You say yes, I do. Yes, I do. And he doesn't. So I think we, sometimes, have people who have been, to some extent, victimized or disrespected and we don't pay attention to them. We don't listen to their issues.
So I think we just going to have to do a lot more listening. And if a person says, across the board, this is offensive, then maybe where there's smoke, there's fire.
Maybe so. We've got to get out of here because we have run out of time. I suppose in one way, you could say this is like when they used to say you're a credit to your race. But…
Oh, wow.

Oh, absolutely. And let me add that he's nice looking and quite the mainstream player that we hope and wish for all African-Americans.

Well, I was joking when I said that, playing on Joe Biden's words, but I don't think that there's any question that Barack Obama stands as the African-American with the best chance of actually winning the Democratic nomination in American history. Would you agree, Donna?

Absolutely. Let me tell you why. He comes across as someone who is not a politician, someone who is anxious to help bring the country together, to help heal divisions, racial divisions, political divisions, cultural divisions. He is someone that has positioned himself in the political mainstream.

Well, Ron Christie, Donna Brazile said he's behind Hillary Clinton in most of the polls, but he's behind by a lot, by 20 or 30 points, and he doesn't have the money that Hillary Clinton has, and he doesn't have the name identification. What does it look like from a Republican point of view?

I think on the Republican side of the fence, that Barack Obama represents a formidable candidate for the Democrats. He is not politics as usual, as so many of the candidates that you see running right now on the Democratic side have been around Washington, have been part of the problem, if you will, some of the discord that a lot of the American people find with politics as usual in Washington.

And I just don't think its Senator Clinton's coronation that we're going to see. I think Senator Obama is going to push her far to the left. Further perhaps than Senator Clinton would have wanted to go. I also think he's going to make her run and run very hard to get that nomination.

The question comes back to money and name I.D. and the black community. Mrs. Clinton in a poll done in New York was leading even among African-Americans over Barack Obama. So Donna Brazile, is that indicative of what you think the national response from the black community will be to Obama?

Well, currently she is leading Mr. Obama by at least 40 points in national polling. She's attracting about 60 percent of African-Americans. He's attracting only 20 percent. His problem, again, is name recognition. Most African-Americans are not familiar with him.

While he gave a very, you know, dynamic speech at the Democratic National Convention, I do believe that it's his challenge, like the challenge of all the other Democrats, is to introduce themselves to black voters and to earn their trust. Barack also needs a couple of good surrogates to go out and make his case.

I was at a meeting recently, one where Senate - Illinois Senate President Emil Jones, who's African-American, was at the DNC Black Caucus, and he used that opportunity not to talk about Obama, his record, his leadership, his strengths, but he used it to basically criticize African-American Democrats who have endorsed, have shown some political support to Hillary Clinton. And the refrain he used was how long, how long will we owe the Clintons. Well, that didn't really help Barack's cause.

I think what he needs right now is people like Jesse Jackson, Jr., Reverend Jesse Jackson, and perhaps many others who are familiar with the African-American community, go out there and make his case.

Ron Christie, when you are looking at this from the Republican side, there is no black person running for the Republican nomination for president. Do you see an absence there? I think Republicans have done a remarkable effort in the last decade of making inroads in the African-American community, not just at the national level but at the state and local level.

If you look just back at this past election, you had Lynn Swann running for governor in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. You had Michael Steele running for the United States Senate in Maryland; you had a wide variety of candidates, Mr. Blackwell in Ohio, who are running for statewide office.
And let me…

Well, Ron Christie - hang on a second, Donna. But Ron Christie, is there one candidate that you can identify right now running as a Republican who's likely to do better than George W. Bush did in 2000 and 2004 in winning a percentage of the black vote? I repeat - George W. Bush, I think, got 11 percent and 16 percent in 2000 and 2004. For president, I think there are a couple of candidates who could appeal to African-Americans, who could equal what President Bush has done. I think Mitt Romney would be one, the governor of Massachusetts. The governor up there has been rather progressive on certain social issues. He has provided universal health care for people living in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. I think that's one individual who might do a lot better in the African-American community, or at least on par with what President Bush has done.

And the second, I would say, would be someone like Mike Huckabee, who is a dark horse in the Republican field, if you will, a very popular governor in the state of Arkansas, and someone who, I think, resonates with people not only of color, but people who - who will resonate with people all around the country.
But if you look at some of the mainstream Republican candidates, I don't see them at this point breaking out of the low teens for the African-American percentage of the vote.

You know, Juan, if Barack Obama was not black, he would be considered one of the most serious threats to the status quo in the Democratic Party. I do believe that his race unfortunately has become a topic of conversation and a distraction. Barack is the future of what black politics will look like at some point in the distant future.

But at this moment in history, he will have to navigate the racial waters and begin to hone in a message that continue to galvanize people, bring them together. I'm excited that he's getting in the race and I'm excited that we have somebody of his caliber and strength and of course of his generation who's willing to speak to the issues and the vision that we hope to see our country go forward with.

On today's Roundtable, DaimlerChrysler announces 13,000 hourly jobs will be cut and Africa may get a media image makeover.

Joining us are E.R. Shipp, professor in journalism at Hofstra University School of Communication, plus John McWhorter, Manhattan Institute senior fellow in public policy. Bush.

So Ron, I'm going to start with you. DaimlerChrysler - 13,000 jobs gone, its Newark, Delaware, plant is going to close. Executives say, okay, we're redesigning, we've got a new business model. But U.S. automakers, are they on their knees? Is this the end of an era, at least the era of the truck and the SUV, if not the era of American autos?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: Well, Farai, I don't think that we're at the end of the era for the U.S. automaker, but U.S. automakers are in a very difficult position right now to remain competitive with the world market. If you look in the United States, the transportation sector accounts for the majority of the petroleum that's used in the United States.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: And breaking that down a little further, cars and light trucks are the largest users of petroleum, given the reliance on foreign supply of oil. And given the spikes of energy costs in the United States, I think the American auto industry is facing the reality that consumers are switching to more fuel-efficient cars. And those gas guzzling light trucks and SUVs, consumers are turning away from those, and as a result the U.S. auto industry is suffering.

Now E.R., there's a lot of talk about China, which seems poised to enter the U.S. auto market. You've got Japanese, Korean, Yugoslavian carmakers. Does this really bode ill for the American car market and for the many people, African-American and of all races, who work in the auto industry?

Professor E.R. SHIPP (Journalism, Hofstra University): Well, in the short term it does. In the long term it may not be such a bad thing to get people thinking about fuel efficiencies and even using public transportation rather than driving everywhere they have to go.

The issue of which workers are going to be affected, I was interested that in your previous segment talking about the debt that people have and how it's very hard to become middle class and to retain middle-class status these days. This is definitely going to be a hit on those people - black, white and otherwise - who have been depending upon the auto industry to give them that leg up in the middle class.

John, I just really wonder, looking at what is happening with the U.S. auto industry. African-Americans, a lot of folks were able to go from high school into the plants and earn a good living. And is there a real undermining of the black community or have we already reacted to the downward slump in terms of the, you know, the good working-class job that seems to be disappearing in this era?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Well, you know, there was a grand period from the '20s into the 1960s when it was possible for a black man, or sometimes a woman, with no education to have a good solid job in an auto plant. And I think we're taught to look to that as the way things should be, when in fact I think we need to think of it more as a matter of who moved my cheese?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: This factory closing is a symbol of the fact that those days unfortunately can't come back, and in a way, in a global sense, so to speak, it's for a good reason because the fewer of those big guzzling cars we produce, the more leverage we'll have on certain rather pressing geopolitical issues elsewhere.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: But this is a wakeup call for us to realize that the old idea of the black father who works for the River Rouge Ford plant in Detroit - that was a good thing. But that's gone and that was actually only for about one-tenth of black American history, and we've coped in other ways.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: And nowadays we need to start looking at other solid working-class jobs of that kind. Like nowadays, when you see a black security guard, that's the equivalent of somebody who used to work in the black factory. We need to look to other jobs like that and adjust. It's an era that is unfortunately and fortunately over, and we just have to face the challenge of the future.
But security guards don't make nearly as much as autoworkers.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Depends on how long you stay as a security guard. And if you become something like a real estate inspector or building inspector, or even if you have a job as a - commercial fisherman is a job that is not closed to black people, and you could start making good money as a commercial fisherman. It's just a matter of imagination, I think.
But we're using up all the fish.
Yeah, that's another whole topic but…

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: Yeah, we will always have (unintelligible)…

But that is very true. Well, you know, I just want to turn to another related issue about money. And E.R., you mentioned coming out of our previous segment the whole idea of Americans in jeopardy because of credit card debt. But now, forward to 2007, Bank of America is offering credit cards to customers without Social Security numbers, many of whom are undocumented immigrants.

Now this is part of a trend by banks across the country to cater to the Latino community. Some are offering checking accounts and mortgages to undocumented immigrants. I guess there's a couple of factors here. One, does this sound like good business? And two, does it kind of tar and feather the Latino community with this image of being undocumented?

Well, it's good business for the banks. They're charging super high interest rates. They're charging fees to apply for these special credit cards. So they're going to make money. For the person on the other end, the consumer, it seems to represent a way to obtain credit, to obtain credit history so that eventually one might even be able to buy a house. That's what some people have said they're working towards.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: (Unintelligible).

But they're going to - they're having to pay a big price. I am conflicted on this because I like to see people with opportunities, but the issue becomes are we winking and nodding and saying we don't care about illegal immigration anymore?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: And we are. And as far as I'm concerned, that's just one of those eggs that we're going to have to break to make the omelet. I think this is the most wonderful thing, because in the larger scheme of things we're talking about micro-credit. And rapacious as those interest rates seem - it's funny, if you look around the world, very poor people have a way of coping with them. And so you combine the capitalist impulse of the evil, cigar-chomping bankers with the initiative of people on the bottom, and next thing you know you have social growth.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: I think that this whole model should be extended even to the lower economic part of the African-American community. Micro-credit is the next big thing, I suspect.
Well, John, what about the political implications? I mean at this point should the U.S. government be involved in anyway with regulating who gets credit if in fact people don't have green cards?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Well, you know the way I feel about it, although I know for many people this would raise hackles, is that those people aren't leaving. And it is unclear to me that there is any kind of technology we could come up with that could keep an appreciable number of them out. So we can argue till the cows come home as to whether or not they should be there and what the meaning of the word amnesty in. In the meantime, they're there, they're leaving places, they're in the schools, they're in the hospital system, and they're not going anywhere.
And their children…

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: You need to be pragmatic.
Their children in many cases are citizens because they were born here.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Exactly, yeah.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: Well, I hate to say the wet blanket into this, gentlemen. But see this is exactly why I'm against with Bank of America is doing. I think that John is absolutely right that micro-credit is the way of the future. And particularly looking at what we've seen with red lining for insurance in African-American communities and the reluctance of some banks perhaps to extend credit to African-Americans, I think that's something that we'd all agree that we should combat. But when you specifically look at a bank, an institution that's in it just to make a buck. They're charging higher interest rates to people who they know or have a high likelihood of knowing are here illegally. That's thwarting our immigration laws. It's against the law.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: I understand that these folks are here, and that's a separate issue. But for a financial institution to decide, well, we're going to make a big buck off a group of people who are poor and desperate and we're going to charge them these rates, I think it's wrong and I think that it's these types of actions by big corporations and big entities that allow illegal immigration to thrive in this country. Because people know that they can come here, they can work, and now they can get credit and they can get a credit card from a major institution.

Well, Ron, you worked in the White House with the vice president. What is the White House thinking about this? Does the White House even consider the implications of this kind of a commercial transaction that takes place on U.S. soil?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: Well, Farai, for having worked for both the vice president and the president of the United States, they are both very concerned about controlling our borders. But I think as you've heard the president, particularly in recent months, talk about the need for comprehensive immigration reform, the president feels very strongly that we need to take steps to address those illegal immigrants who are here in the United States; and that despite some of the calls by members of the House of Representatives to just build a fence and lock everybody out, that we have to deal with the 12 to 16 million undocumented individuals in the country.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: So without speaking for the White House directly, I can tell you that the White House is very concerned about the individuals who are here and that all Americans, recognizing that we have illegal aliens who are in our borders, we have to find a way to make it work so that you're not just throwing people right out and just, you know, showing them the exit. But this credit program is one way, undoubtedly, that a big institution like Bank of America is trying to help folks assimilate into society.
All right, well, in case you're just tuning in, this is NPR's NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya.

We were just talking with Ron Christie, V.P. of the lobbying firm D.C. Navigators and former special assistant to President George W. Bush. We've also got E.R. Shipp, professor and journalism at Hofstra University School of Communication, and John McWhorter, Manhattan Institute senior fellow in public policy.

Let's turn to Africa. I just recently got back. I enjoyed a great trip to southern Africa. But if you go to Nigeria, there is an issue on the table - Africa's media image. There's a big summit, Africa's International Media Summit, good name, very simple. They want to concentrate on the good in Africa and re-brand the continent. Now John, how do you re-brand an entire continent?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Well, for one thing, you don't. And I hate to say this but, you know, having been to Africa more than once, I would say that I think that the negative aspects of Africa are something that require an urgent attention and perhaps more than the fact that they have interesting animals and vibrant cultures, et cetera. I can see why they might want tourism, but the AIDS crisis, the thugocracy crisis, the malaria crisis, the war in the middle of the entire continent that rages on and off.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: I'm not sure that I'm interested in the idea that we are stereotyping Africa or we're focusing on the negative and not the positive and belittling the people or something like that. Unless what this is really about is let's foster tourism to Africa, and that's fine with me. I'm afraid that what's going on in that particular continent is too uniquely awful right now for us to paper it over with pretty words.
I agree.

I think it's not just about tourism, but business in general. And E.R., you were saying you agree but is there a way that this kind of re-branding effort, although it sounds on some level trivial, could help bring more business and could help stimulate the economies and help solve some of the problems that John just outlined.
Well, the problem isn't so much that the economies need stimulating, it's that there needs to be a whole new leadership in many countries.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Yup.

Because the money is there. CNN has been featuring a series of stories this past week about the oil in Nigeria and how much of that money is flowing into the hands of a small group of people, while nearby residents of the area are starving.

So I don't think re-branding Nigeria would mean anything for those people until there's a new leadership and a new morality that's in place. If anything, we are now beginning to focus on Africa as a continent, not as a country. I remember a few years back when this - U.N. had a Security Council meeting or something - and various heads of state would stop by The New York Times. So, one day, I wondered who was there that day because there was all kinds of security outside. And somebody said the president of Africa.
In a newsroom?
Yeah. So I think we've gotten beyond that.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Boy.
But the issue still remains that Africa has a lot of serious problems that a branding of it is not going to really solve.
Ron, what do you think?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: Well, I couldn't agree with my two colleagues more. Having spent a lot of time in Cameroon and having represented the prime minister of Cameroon, you'll don't need a re-branding of the African continent as it relates to tourism and to try to bring dollars in, you need to re-brand some of the leadership in some of these African countries, particularly in Western African and sub-Saharan Africa.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: For goodness sakes, if you look at Cameroon for one, a majority of the people on the government payroll in Cameroon work for Camair, an airline that has been defunct for several years that isn't flying. There is rampant corruption in many of these countries. There is a lot of vigorous, I would say, natural resources that are there to be sold and there to be utilized by the people of these countries.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: But, unfortunately, it seems that in many of these countries the power and the wealth is in the hands of the handful of individuals. And we need to re-brand the governments and re-brand and have democracy and transparency rather than try to re-brand the continent for tourism.
Well, maybe you need to brand the way they used to brand cows in the West. You need to put some heat to their butts and get them to do the right thing.

Well, there certainly are a lot of leadership issues on the continent, but at one point we talked to an entrepreneur who's giving out a leadership prize for people who step down from power. Our own NPR's special correspondent Charlayne Hunter-Gault has talked extensively about how the continent is not just doom and despair.

So what do you think, E.R., could be done positively that acknowledges the need for leadership transition, acknowledges the crisis, but also points out that there is hope and that there are people who are trying to change the systems?

Well, we do hear those stories periodically of specific incidents where positive things are happening. Whether it's Oprah's school opening or some new telecommunications company deciding to do business on the continent.

So yes, we can focus on those things. But I think, as we've all been saying, you can't polish over the fact that this is a continent with a lot of different problems. So what we can do maybe is to have more of the Africa/African-American summits where people get together and talk about problems they're going to try to solve together, and then have some kind of accountability. But you can't just pretend that saying we're an African people and let's throw some money to Africa is going to solve their problems.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: It's hard to (unintelligible) business to a country where one out of three people are sick or dying, for example.

Right. Well, let me - we have almost no time, but I want all three of you to answer this just very briefly: Should African-Americans be more involved in development in Africa? Just give me a yes or a no, Ron.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: Absolutely.
John?

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: I'd like to see a little more concentration on our own community, and then we'll get to Africa. Other people should be taking care of Africa, I think.
I agree more with John, I think.
All right, well that's a wrap. Thanks guys.

speaker_label: Mr. JOHN MCWHORTER (Senior Fellow, Manhattan Institute)
text: Thank you.
Thanks.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: Well, I think this is a very delicate time in foreign policy in the Middle East. Iran has continued to enrich uranium, much to the detriment and much to the concern of the United Nations community. The United Nations, working through the Security Council, has asked Iran to stop their proliferation and enrichment of uranium.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: And I think the United States is looking, as are all nations, to ensure that there is compliance with the U.N. mandate. And if Iran does not comply, then I think the United States will be in a position to seek counsel and to seek alliance with other members in the Security Council to impose sanctions, economic sanctions and other sanctions on Iran.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: But it will be very interesting, I think, to see particularly what Russia and China do - two friends of Iran who are permanent members of the United Nations security council - whether they would block such efforts to impose sanctions.
I mean, do you think they will?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)
text: I think if in fact the report comes out and it says what we believe that it will say, that Iran continues to enrich uranium for purposes other than domestic energy, I think that the international community will be very swift in trying to impose economic and other sanctions to bring Iran back to the negotiating table and make them feel a little bit of pain, not in a military way but from an economic perspective to bring them into compliance.

Marcelo, let's break it down on sanctions for just a second. Iraq was under sanctions for many years. Some human rights advocates argued that it hurt the people but not the president because he had access to the wealth. Zimbabwe's been under sanctions. Again, many people arguing that it's the people who suffer, not the presidents. What do sanctions really do? Are they effective?

speaker_label: Professor MARCELO SUAREZ-OROZCO (Globalization and Education, New York University)
text: Well, we might have also said Cuba has faced sanctions for a long, long time. Well, the preponderance of evidence shows that sanctions are highly symbolic, they're political in the sense that they telecast a message to the parties, to the larger region, to the world at large.

speaker_label: Professor MARCELO SUAREZ-OROZCO (Globalization and Education, New York University)
text: But in fact there is little evidence to suggest that, as a strategy to induce change in terms of the internal dynamics of governmental policy, sanctions are anemic. This is politics, heavy in politics, but it is quite light in terms of consequences other than hurting typically the most vulnerable citizens. It's children, it's the poor folk, the ethnic minorities that tend to pay the price of politicized sanctions. The leadership protects itself.

So Walter, if you've got a situation where Iran is pursuing a nuclear program that the West doesn't like. At this point, Western governments don't seem too eager to try to go in militarily. Sanctions may not work. What are the options?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, D.C. Navigators)

This is NEWS & NOTES. I'm Farai Chideya.
On today's Roundtable, Charles Drew Medical School files a $125 million lawsuit, and the federal government takes on the Walgreen Company.

Joining today's panel are political consultant Walter Fields, economist and author Julianne Malveaux, president and CEO of Last Word Productions. They're both in New York. And right here with me in Washington, D.C., Ron Christie, vice president of the lobbying firm DC Navigators and former special assistant to President George W. Bush.

So thanks for coming on, everybody. And let's go to King/Drew. It's been a big story, especially in the African-American community. So when the troubled King/Drew Medical Center was cut off from the Drew Medical School, some doctors say it was like losing an appendage. Officials at Charles R. Drew University of Medicine and Science say they're going to sue Los Angeles county for $125 million. They're claiming breach of contract from the county, which cut ties between the medical school and a struggling county hospital near Watts late last year.
Julianne, this is a historically black institution. The hospital has been incredibly troubled, but you can't really have a medical school without an associated hospital. How should this play out?

Well, this is such a tragedy, Farai. Of course, King/Drew Hospital was founded in the wake of Watts uprisings. And its closing leaves the community in the same place it was with the Watts uprisings, having to go far away to get medical service.

Of course, The LA Times has been on this story for a really long time, and there's more than enough blame to go around. But the way that the medical residents were treated at Drew University is something that we have to pay attention to, especially with the context of medical disparities in the African-American community, as well as the fact that, Harry Morehouse and Drew were training a disproportionate number of African-American doctors who have difficulty, for whatever reason - part of them, discrimination - getting into other medical schools. So these residents needed to be transitioned in a much better way. And it doesn't seem to me that the county took that into consideration.

Of course, let's be clear. The hospital - we don't even want to go into the list of challenges the hospital had. But the most recent challenge was that they lost $200 million in federal funding because they had nine deficiencies out of 23. Notably, the treatment or the care from the medical school was not one of the deficiencies.

I think that this $125-million lawsuit is an utter-desperation move on the part of the university who's been constrained from what they can do with training because of the way folks have been treated. There could have been some transition move made so that some of these residents could have been trained, done their rotations at UCLA, USC or other places - that was not done. So again, you know, while race is not the main issue here, race is a factor in the way young black doctors were being treated in the trajectory of their careers.

Now, Ron, this is the only historically black medical school west of the Mississippi. Is it really important to save it? Or considering how bad the hospital has been in terms of its care giving, is this just going to be a casualty?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: My number one concern, Farai, is to ensure that those residents - particularly in lower income areas such as Watts - have access to high-quality medical care. My concern, from looking at this complaint very briefly is that the hospital has failed a crucial part of their inspection. It was tied to $200 million worth of federal funds. And if you look at poor oversight in their radiology and surgery departments, the federal government said that they were going to restrict funds if these standards were not met, and they were not delivering the quality of care that was necessary to have an accreditation.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: So I am very concerned. We must have access to high-quality health care in our African-American communities and our urban areas, as well as our rural areas around the United Stats, but race shouldn't play a part. If, in fact, that these students are not in a hospital that is up to standards, that is up to par, that is up to a medically and board-certified standard, then I think it should shut its doors, because then, what are you going to if you're training people that have improper access to equipment? In other words, they're using faulty equipment or if they're using equipments that aren't up to standards. That's what concerns me.
Walter, is this lawsuit the right way to go about fixing this problem?

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: I think it's their only recourse. You know, I've followed the story for some time in the LA Times, and they did an incredible job, and it's a really tragic story. I think you have to separate issues of care from financial management. And what I'm concerned about is the only teaching hospital teaching black practitioners on the West Coast, that you cut off that needed supply, because our community -there's still an issue of access to primary care.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: And I think it's critically important for the university to have a relationship with a teaching hospital, but a teaching hospital that is within the community of the population that looks like the residents in that university. So I would hope that there is some middle ground here that allows the university to restore relationship with the hospital because I think if you - Julianne talked about the origins of this hospital, it was put there to serve a purpose. And that if now you're cutting off that pipeline of black medical practitioners who can practice in that community and serve that community, we've got a serious problem.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: And I think the audit, while it showed financial mismanagement, from what I remember from reading The LA Times series, there weren't many questions raised about quality of care.
Actually, Walter, there were, unfortunately…

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: Okay.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: Yes, there were.

I mean, the unfortunate thing is that, malpractice - the amount of money that was paid out of King/Drew for malpractice in a four-year period was $20 million. The closest hospital, the UCLA Harbor Hospital, $11 million - similar size, similar budget.

Just about every indicators show that there were care-related issues. There was also an issue in that community as the demographic was changing that there was not enough Spanish language access. But here's the thing: the bigger issue is that there was enormous overcrowding, which is a function of being located in an inner-city area, where people are getting their primary health care in the emergency room.

But there are - this - my analysis is that three things are happening here. One is civil service rigidity - people couldn't fire anybody. So you have one man who is like an emergency room tech at night, and in rehab - in one of these halfway house during the day.

Now, I'm not sure that I want him sewing me up, you know, for the record. You had, so you have civil service rigidity, you have some incompetence, but you also have the issue of race - in other words, that's all they deserve - and you have a tally board of supervisors who sat on it.

Good people, James Hahn, who was a champion initially, not moving aggressively when he was alive. When you saw - they began to get complaints in 1977, five years after the hospital opened. Yvonne Brathwaite Burke, known as a conciliator - I don't know if you need a conciliator when a hospital is spiraling down…

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: Well, one thing I would, though, do, though, is be careful about tying the issue of malpractice claims and care. You know, I was the former director of public affairs for the New York trial lawyers. So malpractice litigation, it's something that I do know something about, and I think…
But you know, the homies did not have good lawyers…

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: Well…
…so there had to be some…

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: Well, some of it is also driven by other factors. And I think the tragedy here is that the hospital was providing a level of care that would not have been provided had not that hospital been there. We need to figure out…
All right, well, I want to…

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: Whether this…

That's questionable. I mean, the - the hospital's nickname was Killer King, okay? And, I mean, that's the nickname that people referred to in the news - in reputable newspapers. I'm not, you know, I think it's a mixed piece, and I'm sorry the hospital isn't there.

And I think a lot of people are, you know, to blame for this, but I think the bottom line, in terms of the school, is that the county did the school wrong. There could have been something transitional so that those medical residents, who we will desperately need - so that those African-American, Latino medical residents were able to have some other training function for themselves as their careers are moving.

All right, we're going to have to wrap this topic up. It's obviously one generating a lot of heat, and it's health care, a huge issue. In case you're just tuning in, this is NPR's NEWS & NOTES. I am Farai Chideya. We were last listening to Julianne Malveaux, president and CEO of Last Word Productions, Inc., political consultant Walter Fields and Ron Christie, VP of the lobbying firm, DC Navigators and former special assistant to President George W. Bush.

I want to move on to the Walgreen Company. They EEOC - Equal Employment Opportunity Commission - is suing the drugstore retailer, claiming that it assigned employees to locations according to race, denying them promotions for the same reason. They investigated a complaint in Florida. You know, and so now, we have, after many different sort of class-action suits - Coca-Cola recently made some moves to really deal with its own diversity issues - a big, big, issue with Walgreens. Now, how much damage do you think, Ron, that this suit does?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: I think it does a lot of damage. It would be one thing if this was an isolated incident with Walgreens and allegations of discrimination. As a lawyer, I can tell you, not knowing what all the facts are, I don't want to make any sweeping pronouncements, but this troubles me.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: You have the EEOC office in St. Louis, you have the EEOC office in Miami, looking at the assignment of individuals, and apparently, it's being done so -based solely on the color of their race and the color of their skin, I should say. And the EEOC tried to get a settlement. They tried to work voluntarily with Walgreens. They were unable to reach an agreement with them. And so they had to file a suit under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: So I think that this is a very troubling allegation. It's very troubling - a seeming pattern with this particular drugstore, and I hope that we get all the facts out and that a situation is reached that if, in fact, that there has been systematic racism or systematic discrimination, this company and its employees are held fully responsible.

Julianne, maybe you can tell us a little about the government's role in this. In some cases there are class action lawsuits that are brought directly by employees. This is a government action. Is that something that is surprising? Encouraging?

Well, it's interesting, Farai, because there is also a class action lawsuit that individual African-American employees have brought together without EEOC. EEOC's job is to conciliate. And coming out of this conservative administration, frankly, with all their rhetoric about race neutrality, you have to conclude that Walgreens have been pretty bad off to get EEOC to file.

EEOC does not do this often. I mean, they will investigate; they will also attempt to get you to do some settlement. Often you'll hear that, you know, people are getting some small sum and that some programs are being instituted. And that is usually by EEOC urging.

So when the Equal Employee Opportunity Commission, with the majority of its commissioners having been appointed by a conservative Republican administration, says we're going to go ahead with this discrimination lawsuit, I would say this is one case where the fire preceded the smoke.
Walter?

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: No, it had to be that. I mean, I was shocked because there's been a drought at the EEOC for some time now, and this goes back to the Reagan administration, which gutted the EEOC. And our friend Justice Thomas was leading efforts there. So I think that we must have a case of, you know, extreme situations when you have them pursuing this matter against Walgreens.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: And I think it's a breath of fresh air because, quite frankly, across the country there are cases of discrimination in the workplace that do not receive fair hearing in our courts. The courts have been hostile to employment discrimination suits. So I think it's great that the federal agency responsible for this is stepping up to the plate on a situation with a company that has, you know, national implications.

I want to move on to one last topic getting huge amount of play. Yesterday, Congress held hearings on what some might call credit card abuse. With consumer's crunched by debt, the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations is looking into complaints of unjustified fees and penalties on credit card bills.
Senator Carl Levin is chairman of the subcommittee, and he says credit card companies need to lighten up.

Senator CARL LEVIN (Democrat, Michigan) Stop charging consumers a fee to pay their bills and stop imposing abusive fees and excessive penalty interest rates. As one Michigan businessman expressed it to the subcommittee, I don't blame the credit card issuers for putting me into debt, but I do blame them for keeping me there.

Now there are other studies and figures showing that Americans are actually spending more money than they make, so it's not really a surprise that people are in credit card debt. But should it be illegal to pursue some of the strategies that credit card companies have in order to put additional fines and to raise interest rates at will?
Julianne, you're an economist, what do you think?

I think that Levin is right on the money here. This is an absurd situation, Farai. It's, you know, everybody who's in business is entitled to make a profit, but this is where you have literally usury. In addition to people paying some 30 percent interest if they missed a payment or two, then you have a $25 to $50 late fee that will be imposed time and time and time again. That's how the gentleman in question who was testifying got into trouble.

Then you've got this thing called the universal default clause, which means, okay, I pay my American Express bill on time every month, but I don't pay Visa on time. So American Express accesses me through Visa and now they say I'm going to charge you more money. So the universal default clause says one credit problem with one isolated company can wreck my entire payment schedule with every company.

Again, credit card companies bare some culpability here. Farai, in 2004, four billion credit card solicitations went out; there are 300 million Americans. The average person got eight credit card solicitations. You know, teenagers get them. College students get them. And of course then they get the card and then they use it, that's why they get it, you know, and then we pass this bankruptcy legislation that makes it more difficult for people to declare bankruptcy. We prioritize the repayment of credit cards over the payment of child support.

So Levin was right on time to bring these people in and to at least let them know that people are watching. The laws vary state by state about percentage of interest, but no one has began to regulate all these late and ancillary fees. And that's something I think that's legitimate for the Congress and state legislatures to look at.
Walter, though, in business isn't it really, as the phrase goes, what the market will bear?

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: No. Because this is the equivalent of piling on in sandlot football, where someone is tackled and then you get 30 other people to jump on the pile. This is what credit card companies do. They just pile on and they pile on these fees. And as someone who ran a business for 11 years, I will tell you dealing with them is extremely difficult because, first of all, you can't understand the terms of the contract. If you read the terms of your credit card, you can get someone who is an expert in contract law…
I've had, like, five pages show up. It's, like, we've made a change, five pages of…

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: You can't read it.
…fine print.
What does it mean? What does it mean? Tell me in English what it means.

speaker_label: Mr. WALTER FIELDS (CEO and Publisher, North Star Network)
text: And I think Julianne makes a point in terms of the aggressiveness of marketing of credit card companies. My daughter is eight and she has received mail from credit card companies. It's ludicrous what's happening out here in terms of they reel you in, they suck you in, you get the card and you make payments. You can even pay off your credit card and they will charge you a fee based upon the balance that you were paid off. It is absolutely ridiculous, and now finally Congress looks like they're going to do something about it.
Ron, we'll end with you on that point. Is there an appetite in Congress, in the government, to make some changes in the law?

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: Well, I think there is an appetite to have oversight hearings, which as Walter said, it seems to be is long overdue. But these credit card companies have been piling on year after year. They make a lot of money. I don't begrudge anybody who works hard for making a profit. But for having been one who in college got a lot of these solicitation letters, applied for the cards, used the cards, ran up a lot of debt, and then you start paying off the debt and you still get charged interest fees - from a personal standpoint I can tell you enough is enough.

speaker_label: Mr. RON CHRISTIE (Vice President, DC Navigators)
text: These guys need to be held accountable. And those small, little, teeny tiny pieces of paper that you get with your credit card statement, you can get a magnifying glass to read it, you still can't understand it, and they're just making money hand over fist. Enough is enough.

And so, he's claimed 31 - full or partial responsibility in 31 terrorist acts, including attempts on the lives of both Presidents Clinton. And I believe - on presidents.

speaker_label: Ms. JULIANNE MALVEAUX (CEO, Last Word Productions Inc.)
text: So he's made several claims that we're not sure we can validate. I think that this is the tip of the iceberg, and certainly so much of this, Farai, has been kept secret.
